metadata.title: “Hot-headed” students? Scientific literacy, perceptions and awareness of climate change in 15-year olds across 54 countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata (15-year-olds in grades 7+) combined with country-level environmental indicators. Sampling follows PISA’s stratified two-stage design (schools sampled first, then students within schools), and the authors explicitly state that weights are included to support representative inferences across participating countries. For the cross-country component, they use senate weights (rather than final student weights) to adjust for differing first-stage sampling probabilities and country non-response, so each country contributes more equally to the analysis. The analytic sample is further restricted to students who answered the greenhouse-gas awareness item and are included only in a complete-case analysis; no replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds (grades 7+) in science as the senior subject, restricted to students who responded to the greenhouse-gas awareness item (ST09201TA: “How informed are you about the increase of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere?”). From 519,334 original observations across 69 countries, the final complete-case analysis includes 336,396 students from 54 countries; participants from the listed 15 countries (Argentina, Albania, Algeria, Georgia, Indonesia, Jordan, Kosovo, Lebanon, Macedonia, Malta, Moldova, Romania, Thailand, Trinidad and Tobago, Viet Nam) were excluded. Additional missing-data patterns reduced the available sample (e.g., missingness related to enjoyment of science, climate-ordered, instrumental motivation to science, and interest in broad science), and the authors report that the analysis is complete-case only (multiple imputation was attempted but did not converge).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds; grades 7+; ST09201TA awareness item)
main_findings.target_variable: Awareness of increase in greenhouse gases (ordered categories)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bayesian multilevel ordered logistic (proportional odds) model; reported effects as odds ratios and probability-scale credible intervals (no ML accuracy/AUC/RMSE). Largest effect: PISA science score odds-ratio 4.91–5.96; females vs males odds-ratio 0.82–0.92; enjoyment odds-ratio 1.37–1.40; interest odds-ratio 1.36–1.39.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study leveraged PISA science score (plausible values), enjoyment of science, interest in broad science topics, cultural possessions at home, and sex of respondent to model students’ ordered awareness of the increase in greenhouse gases, finding that higher scientific literacy strongly increases the likelihood of reporting being well informed while females report lower awareness on average. This indicates that strengthening science learning experiences and students’ engagement with science may improve environmental awareness, though the results are correlational and based on self-reported awareness rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-olds (grades 7+) across 54 countries, modeling students’ self-reported awareness of the increase in greenhouse gases (ST09201TA) as an ordered four-category outcome. The authors fit a Bayesian multilevel ordered logistic proportional-odds model with school- and country-varying intercepts, using senate weights to address cross-country sampling and non-response differences. Missingness is handled via complete-case analysis (multiple imputation was attempted but did not converge). Scientific literacy (PISA science score, modeled via 10 plausible values) is the strongest predictor: students scoring one SD higher are about 34.5% more likely to report being more informed (odds-ratio 4.91–5.96). Enjoyment of science and interest in broad science topics each show sizable positive associations (odds-ratios ~1.37–1.40), while females are less likely on average (odds-ratio 0.82–0.92). Limitations include reliance on self-reported awareness and the absence of causal identification.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning algorithms; it uses a Bayesian multilevel ordered logistic regression framework (with plausible values for the science score) rather than ML predictive modeling. Therefore, ml_techniques is intentionally empty and no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable.
